Testimony for LD 2147 (Upward Bound River Valley Bill)
By: Abby Waceken
01/21/2026
Good morning, everyone. My name is Abby Waceken and I am a resident of Farmington, Maine. I am here not as a representative of any-. institution, or my employer, but as a
concerned citizen who has seen first-hand the impact of this particular Upward Bound
program.
I started my journey working for UMF Upward Bound as a summer staff member in
2020, and then went on to be hired as a full-time staff member in 2022. I have worked
in my role as an academic counselor for the last 4 years and in that time, I have seen many lives changed for the better by our Upward Bound program. This September, my
colleagues and I received news that both shocked and devastated us; we learned,
through a non-continuation notice, that one of our two grants would be prematurely ended on October 1 of 2025.
This grant, called the "River Valley" grant, served 60 students in 6 high schools across
western Maine. What this meant is that of the 139 students that we would typically serve in our program, 60 of them lost all access to the resources and help provided by Upward
Bound, access that they had been promised until their high school graduation. As you
can imagine, our students were quite distraught when receiving this news. For many of them, Upward Bound is so much more than just a college prep program; it is a lifeline, a safe place, and a CRUCIAL support system while they're in high school.
These students are intelligent, motivated, and desperately want to attend college and earn a degree. But, there are a lot of barriers to higher education when you live in
poverty and nobody in your family has ever attended college. Of the students that we
9!
served through the River Valley grant, 66% of them were considered to be "low-income,
which meant that their fami1y's total income for the year did not exceed 150 percent of the federal poverty level amount. To put this into perspective, in 2026 this would mean
that a family of 3 would have to have a yearly income of $40,980 or less; A family of 5
would have to have an income of less than $58,020.
Because of the devastating effects of poverty, many of our students have experienced firsthand things that no human should ever have to go through. I've personally worked
with students that have experienced traumas such as food insecurity (not having enough to eat), a lack of access to proper medical/ dental care, having utilities shut off or disconnected at home, homelessness (living in a motel), evictions or frequent moving,

not having money to afford new clothing and shoes when needed, a lack of access to reliable transportation, and so much more. For many of these students, education is the only way for them to escape these dire circumstances.
The data tells us that programs like Upward Bound work; UB students are more than
twice as likely to earn a bachelor's degree by age 24 compared to other students in the
lowest income bracket. Many of our alumni tell us that they never would have made it to college without the support provided by our UB program. This bill is being presented by Senator Jill Duson, an Upward Bound alumni herself who knows just how valuable these programs are. LD 2147 would fund the River Valley grant for one more year. With this funding, River Valley students would be able to access the Upward Bound resources
and help that they have been denied since October of 2025. This assistance includes
FREE academic counseling, tutoring, college visits, help with the college application
process, fee waivers for college applications + the SAT, as well as the opportunity to
attend a residential summer program that takes place on the UMF campus each
summer. But most importantly, this bill would restore our River Valley students' hopes and dreams for the future. Thank you all for your time and consideration on this matter.

Good morning, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Inembers of the Education and

10057552:
Colleen Brown Whiting LD 2147
To the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs,
I am writing as a Maine resident and taxpayer regarding LD 2147.
I support the goal of this bill, which is to strengthen career and college readiness for Maine students. Preparing young people for the workforce, especially in high-need regions, is one of the smartest investments this Legislature can make. However, I am deeply concerned that this bill limits funding to only Androscoggin and Oxford Counties while leaving other high-need rural areas, including Washington County, out of the equation.
Washington County faces some of the highest rates of poverty, the fewest postsecondary and career training options, and some of the longest travel distances to access education and employment. Our students are just as deserving of career pathways, technical training, and college readiness supports as students in more politically visible regions of the state.
When workforce investment is targeted only to certain counties, it sends a message that some Maine students matter more than others. That is not how statewide economic development should work.
If Maine is serious about growing its workforce, keeping young people in the state, and supporting rural communities, this bill should be expanded to include all high-need counties, including Washington County and other rural regions that face even greater barriers to opportunity.
I urge the committee to either amend LD 2147 to make this funding available statewide or to include additional counties that face similar or greater challenges.
Thank you for considering my testimony and for your work on this important issue.
196388:
Elizabeth Hansen

Regarding LD 2147, An Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career

Readiness of Certain Students in Andiroscoggin and Oxford Counties.

Q

January 21, 2026

Good morning members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is Elizabeth Hansen and I am a resident of Farmlngton. I am here to speak in favor of LD2147, "An
Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career Readiness of Certain Students in
Androscoggin and Oxford Counties." I'm appearing on my own behalf and on my own time; for the sake of transparency, I am a current employee at UMaine Farmington with the Upward Bound program. All of my comments today are my own, and are in no way an official statement
from the university and shouldn't be considered as such.

Upward Bound programs fall under the umbrella of TRIO, which, contrary to what the name implies, now includes eight federally funded programs. The purpose of Upward Bound is to provide participants with the skills and motivation necessary to complete a program of secondary education and to enter and succeed in a program of post-secondary education.
Essentially, we are helping students graduate from high school and continue on to enroll in a
certificate, associate, or bachelors degree program.

Students that participate in Upward Bound programs must meet one of more of the
following qualifications:

0 Be first-generation: an individual whose parents or legal guardians did not complete a bachelor's degree or who lived with and was supported by only one parent who did not
complete a bachelor's degree
0 Be low-income: family taxable income did not exceed 150% of the poverty level amount
as set by the federal government 0 Have another academic need: This could include rural isolation, a documented learning
disability, living in a predominantly low-income community, lack of opportunity, support and/or guidance to take challenging college preparation courses, or a lack of confidence, self-esteem, and/or social skills

Any of these unique qualifications on their own have been shownto make post secondary attainment more challenging, and many Upward Bound participants are eligible multiple ways, stacking the odds even more against them. This is the case for many students
that were being supported through the River Valley grant.

I am here today because I truly believe in these programs. This is my second
professional role with a TRIO project - I was most recently working at a college in Oklahoma in their Student Support Services program, and it was there that I saw the transformative power
that TRIO had for those students. When I returned to my home state of Maine last summer for
this role at UMaine Farmington, I was excited and honored to become part of the legacy of these programs. Upward Bound at UMaine Farmington has existed since 1982 with the Foothills Upward Bound grant, which is still operating and supports 8 other high schools; the River Valley

Upward Bound grant became an additional component to the program in 2012 supporting the
six schools included in this bill. This demonstrates decades of successfully meeting the objectives of the Upwa�rd Bound program, and it has been disheartening, to say the least, to
witness and be affected by sweeping decisions made by the Department of Education.

Statistics from the River Valley grant demonstrate its success. Through participation in
the project, the majority of students meet academic requirements of having a 2.5 GPA or higher,
over half meet or exceed the proficient level on state assessments in reading/language arts and math, minimal cases of students dropping out of high school, and students persisting to the next grade level or graduation as appropriate. lnu the current 5-year grant cycle, nearly 3/4th of participants enrolled in some form of post secondary education immediately following high school graduation. This program works!

Having to break the news to my team, and then to our summer staff, school liaisons and
community partners was extremely hard. Having to share this news with River Valley students
was heartbreaking. We experienced a range of emotions - confusion, anger, sadness, isolation,
fear, disappointment, discomfort. Students were in tears; they shared their fears that this would
mean they would not make it to college now. Some students cannot even afford the college application fees, which are waived nationwide by many institutions for students that participate in Upward Bound. They are now missing out on the sen/ices and support offered by the
program, such as academic preparation for college, free tutoring, college visits, assistance with applying for student financial aid and scholarships, other financial literacy education, and a
residential summer program to help prevent "summer melt." The latter occurs significantly
higher in low income high school graduates, where those that intend to start college in the fall ultimately fail to enroll due to administrative hurdles, financial confusion, and lack of support. It is a major retention challenge, often stemming from missing deadlines, financial aid issues, feeling overwhelmed, or not knowing how to access support. This is a large component of our
summer program that River Valley students will no longer have the chance to participate in.
We care deeply about students in Maine, and we want to help close the gap for those
that want to get to college or obtain professional skills. Another year of funding to support eligible students from Buckfield Junior-Senior High School, Dirigo High School, Edward Little High School, Mountain Valley High School, Oxford Hills Comprehensive High School and Telstar High School in Androscoggin and Oxford counties would allow us to continue this work, and would be a strong indicator to these deserving students that Mainers take care of each other.

I am very appreciative to Senator Duson for her presentation of this bill, the

cosponsorship from Representative Murphy, Senators Bennett and Bickford, and

Representative Hepler, as well as to the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs for

hearing these testimonies today. Thank you very much.

Testimony by Jason Judd, Ed.D., Executive Director, Educate Maine
To The Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs on Wednesday, January 21, 2026, 10:00am
In Support of
LD 2147: An Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career Readiness of Certain Students in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
I am writing to express my support for LD 2147: An Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career Readiness of Certain Students in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties. Educate Maine is a business-led education organization focused on increasing education attainment. Our mission is to ensure that Maine people are prepared to succeed in education and careers, and that all Maine people reach their highest educational potential.
My understanding is that this bill will support high school students from six schools in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties with academic support and college and career preparation services. The University of Maine at Farmington's River Valley Upward Bound program served these students in the past until a federal grant was recently cancelled. When I was a high school student attending school in Somerset County, I was able to attend UMF's Upward Bound program where I received academic support and college and career preparation services. This program was instrumental in helping me pursue postsecondary education as a low-income and firstgeneration college student. Thanks to the support of UMF's program, I've been able to pursue a variety of postsecondary degrees including two degrees from campuses of the University of Maine System and one from Northeastern University. Students in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties should have these same opportunities.
First-generation students and students from low-income families do not attend postsecondary education at the same rates as their peers. Educate Maine publishes the Education Indicators Report for Maine which includes a snapshot of important data about Maine's education system. Metrics include Maine's high school graduation data, post-secondary enrollment data, post-secondary persistence data, and post-secondary graduation data. According to Maine's most recent data, 57% of Maine high school graduates enroll in postsecondary education. Higher income students enroll in college at a much higher rate than their economically disadvantaged peers (the gap is 20 points). It is also important to note that only 58% of Maine college students graduate within 6 years of enrollment. The completion rates of college students are 28 points more for higher income students versus their economically disadvantaged peers. This data highlights the need for additional support for students from lowincome families to help increase enrollment and graduation rates for Maine students.
There are a variety of best practices happening in communities across Maine to help students improve academically and prepare them for success in postsecondary education. It is important that we continue to invest in programs that support low-income and first-generation students. The various Upward Bound programs and other TRIO programs available at Maine's higher education institutions are wonderful examples of these best practices happening across Maine. In addition, Maine's support of early college is an essential program to help

JMG programs across Maine also support students to successfully enter postsecondary education and the workforce. These are just a few examples of programs that we should support to help improve postsecondary enrollment, persistence, and completion for Maine students.
I encourage members to support this bill and continue to prioritize best practices that can help all learners be prepared for postsecondary education and the workforce.

To: Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and Honorable Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
From: Lynn Ploof-Davis
Re: Support for LD 2147, "An Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career Readiness of Certain Students in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties"
Date: 1/21/2026, 10:00 am
Introduction Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the committee, my name is Lynn Ploof-Davis and I live in Wilton. I retired from a 43-year career with Upward Bound on June 6. I am writing to testify in support of LD 2147. I would like to thank sponsors Senator Duson and Representative Murphy and cosponsors Senator Bennett, Senator Bickford, and Representative Hepler for their foresight and understanding of the complex situation that led to the abrupt defunding of the River Valley Upward Bound program at the University of Maine at Farmington by the US Department of Education. This action left 60 low-income and first-generation high school students with the devastating news that they would no longer have the help and support of Upward Bound to pursue their dreams of a college education.
I began my career in the fall of 1982 with a trip in my yellow VW beetle to Telstar High School for my first meetings with Upward Bound students. In spite of the fact that I ended up in NH and had to search for a pay phone, those first meetings were the beginning of a long career of advising students, administrating TRIO grants and advocating for equity in high education.
In those early years, Buckfield, Dirigo, Mt. Valley, Oxford Hills, and Telstar were part of the original UB grant. As time went on, and the project dealt with funding limitations and target area contraction, we lost the ability to provide services to those schools. It was the relentless advocacy of an RSU 10 professional who was both an administrator and Upward Bound alum that convinced us to write a second Upward Bound grant, funded in September of 2012. Since that time, students in six schools have accessed services to help them reach their educational and career goals. They have attended robust and challenging academic summer programs, gone on college trips, received individualized academic advising, received support for their families, and gained the confidence and skills to allow them to be them successful in higher education.
The research is clear. Every metric in education, from GPA, to high school graduation, to college enrollment, and college graduation, is more likely with participation in Upward Bound. UB students also tend to remain close to home which leads them becoming active and contributing citizens in their communities.

An additional year of funding from the state of Maine would arrive at a critical time and allow the TRIO professionals at UMF to begin the process of writing and submitting a grant for the next competition, in 2027. More importantly, it would reignite the hopes and dreams of 60 students whose dreams were crushed last fall.
Thank you for your time and for the opportunity to share my perspective. I urge the committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 2147.

University of Maine System Testimony In Support of
LD 2147, An Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career Readiness of Certain Students in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties -- Presented by UMS Chief
External & Governmental Affairs Officer Samantha Warren -- January 21, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs: My name is Sam Warren and I am the Chief External & Governmental Affairs Officer for the University of Maine System (UMS) and a proud
graduate of the University of Maine at Farmington (UMF).
Our System is the state's most powerful engine of educational attainment and economic
mobility. Consistent with this, UMS serves 80% of the more than 6,000 TRIO recipients in the state ---- one-third of whom are middle and high school students who are not currently enrolled in
Maine's public universities and may ultimately pursue postsecondary education elsewhere.
1R_lQ_ is the suite of federally funded programs administered by the U.S. Department of
Education (U.S. ED) that prepares students who are low-income, first-generation, or have a
disability for college and careers. All of Maine's public undergraduate universities have active
TRIO programs, with some, such as my alma mater UMF, selected by U.S. ED to support multiple TRIO programs because of their proven track record supporting student success.
Upward Bound is one of these TRIO programs that UMF has effectively delivered since 1980. It
is focused on supporting high school graduation and college-going for secondary students who
are from families that are low-income (i.e., $48,225 or less annual household income for a family of four) or in which neither parent holds a bachelor's degree.
In 2012, UMF launched its River Valley Upward Bound program to serve students in six Oxford
and Androscoggin County high schools (Mountain Valley, Telstar, Dirigo, Edward Little,
Buckfield, and Oxford Hills Comprehensive). Through this program, UMF has provided eligible
students with life-changing counseling and advising, college/career exploration, support
applying for college and accessing financial aid, an annual summer residential experience at
UMF (one-week or five-week options), and a college transition bridge week program. These
services are offered at no cost to participating students and their families -- for the benefit of the
region and beyond. For example, as part of their career exploration activities last summer, participating students provided nearly 1,000 hours of community service at area organizations, including an assisted living facility, an early childhood education center, and a veterinary clinic.
On nearly all measures for which UMF must report outcomes to the federal government, River
Valley Upward Bound exceeded federal goals and even state outcomes, with higher
secondary school grade point averages and rates of graduation, college-going, and college
completion. For example, the 2023-24 cohort achieved a 100% high school graduation rate, well above the state average of 88%, and more than two-thirds pursued postsecondary
education, also above the state average.
Given these impressive outcomes, we were deeply disappointed when U.S. ED notified UMF
University of Maine - University of Maine at Augusta - University of Maine at Farmington - University of Maine at Fort Kent University of Maine at Machias - University of Maine at Presque Isle - University of Southern Maine - University of Maine School of Law

in September that it was canceling the two years remaining on the grant supporting River Valley Upward Bound. Our System's formal request for reconsideration was unfortunately
unsuccessful. As a result, UMF no longer provides Upward Bound services to students formerly
in its River Valley program, though its Western Maine Foothills Upward Bound program is currently active and the university remains an accessible, affordable local option for central and western Maine students to pursue high-quality, high-value higher education and opportunity.
Our System is grateful for the outpouring of support for the students, families, and schools
impacted by this program termination. We appreciate Sen. Duson and her bipartisan, bicameral colleagues recognizing the incredible impact of UMF River Valley Upward Bound and
responding to this devastating loss by proposing to restore some services through LD 2147, An
Act to Provide Funding to Improve the College and Career Readiness of Certain Students in Androscoggin and Oxford Counties.
As this Committee is aware, our System has had more than 130 federal awards paused or
terminated over the past year. We have collaborated with Maine's Congressional Delegation,
federal agencies, and other key partners to restore nearly 100 of these awards. When our appeals have been unsuccessful, we have worked to mitigate impacts and move forward
with education and research of vital importance to Maine and the nation. We are also

We have not looked to the Legislature to replace lost federal funding, nor does UMS typically
seek State appropriations for local initiatives. However, the River Valley Upward Bound program's service area has lower-than-state-average income levels, reading and math proficiency, and rates of high school graduation and postsecondary degree attainment. If the Legislature provided one-time funding to support students in the impacted schools, our System is committed to deploying those dollars in a high-impact manner consistent with the proven
strategies of UMF Upward Bound to build college and career readiness and the critical
workforce pipeline that area employers depend on.
Additionally, as the Legislature considers how to support these and similar students across the state, we encourage increasing the ongoing investment in early college -- the State's existing program to raise college aspirations, promote academic achievement, and grow the size and skill of the Maine workforce. Through early college, thousands of students annually take courses through our public universities and Maine's community colleges while they are in high school, for credit and for free. Doing so helps them develop confidence, build study skills, and see postsecondary education as a place where they belong and will succeed. For example,
graduation rates for rural students who enrolled in UMS early college and then in our public
universities were 12 percentage points higher than those of their peers who did not participate.
l thank you for your ongoing support of the University of Maine System and our statewide efforts to promote prosperity through door-opening postsecondary education. I welcome your
questions.
